card.hook: Picture a red-and-gold pagoda, a long climb of steps and the whole city stretched out below, all in one phone frame. That's the view from the road, before you've climbed a single step.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Canyon Road and Woolbright Drive, on the sidewalk on the left at the turn into Woolbright Drive. Face north-west and the temple's stairs and pagoda rise above the road. That route comes from a 2011 report, so it may have changed.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the stairs, the pagoda and the city view in one go. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the temple. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the pagoda roofs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the pagoda on an upper line and keep the city and sea view in the lower part of the frame.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the colourful roofs than midday. Opening hours differ between listings, so check before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take one by the large green dragon near the entrance, on the way toward the central hall. A guide calls it the biggest dragon on the grounds and the best place for pictures. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone offers it, and let the dragon carving fill the background over your shoulder. You can also pose in the wishing jars area to the right of the main temple, where photos are allowed and the temple buildings sit behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo at the main staircase out front, with you on the steps and the temple rising above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone away inside the main hall and prayer halls, and don't photograph the saint statues. Bring ID for the guardhouse, and motorcycles can't enter. Expect lots of staircases and pathways, so be ready for a moderate workout.
card.challenge: Count the 81 steps as you climb, then snap the one you swear is number 81.
card.good_to_know: Cebu's Chinese Filipino community built the temple in 1972, and it sits about 110 metres above sea level. Devotees climb its 81 steps, one for each chapter of the Taoist scriptures. The entrance was built as a replica of the Great Wall of China.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Canyon Road and Woolbright Drive, on the sidewalk on the left at the turn into Woolbright Drive. Face north-west and the temple's stairs and pagoda rise above the road. That route comes from a 2011 report, so it may have changed.

card.hook: You're in the middle of a business district, and there's a big, leafy tree sitting in a garden right in front of you. That surprise is the whole picture.
card.stand_here: Stand on The Terraces at Ayala Center Cebu, up on the upper balcony. Face out over the landscaped garden and the large tree.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the whole garden, the tree and the buildings around it. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tree canopy or people on the stairs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the big tree on one of the third lines, with the buildings framing it and the balcony rail kept low or out of the shot.
card.best_time: Golden hour (the hour after sunrise or before sunset) is lovely, and so is after dark when the decorative lights come on. The view is wide and open, so it works at other times too. The mall is very busy, so go early if you want fewer people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the balcony above The Terraces, facing the gardens, with the iconic tree and the complex behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if yours has it, to squeeze more green into the background. The wide stairs at the entrance from The Terraces are a good second spot, with several angles and good natural light.
card.rules_and_safety: The Terraces is part of a private shopping mall, so check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules on photography or professional shoots. Stalls and events can block parts of the view, so look around for a clear angle first.
card.challenge: Find a clear angle with the tree on a third line, then wait for one stranger to walk down the stairs so your photo has a little scale.
card.good_to_know: Ayala Center Cebu opened in November 1994 and was the first Ayala mall outside Metro Manila. The Terraces opened on 30 October 2008, on the site of the mall's old lagoon area, and now has food and drink places. A big redevelopment of the mall, including its parks and gardens, was planned for 2024 to 2026, so the layout may look different from older photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on The Terraces at Ayala Center Cebu, up on the upper balcony. Face out over the landscaped garden and the large tree.

card.hook: The best thing about Magellan's Cross is the building around it. Its little arches work like picture frames, and the cross sits right in the middle of one.
card.stand_here: Stand on Plaza Sugbo, next to the Basilica del Santo Niño. Walk about a minute south-east to just outside one of the pavilion's arches and face the cross.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from just outside the arch, so you get the cross and the painted dome ceiling together. For the whole pavilion with the basilica towers behind it, step back across the plaza and try zoom 0.5x. If railings, scaffolding or people get in the way, zoom 2x picks out the cross through the opening.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the pavilion's sides straight, and tap the cross so it stays sharp.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Take a few frames in case people walk through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the plaza side, just outside one of the arches, and take a step back so the pavilion fills the frame behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the pavilion over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand out on the open plaza facing the pavilion, so the Basilica del Santo Niño facade shows up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The pavilion is closed to the public right now, so check the current situation before you go. Selfies are fine, but keep a respectful distance from the cross and from anyone praying. Drones are prohibited here, and keep your valuables secure on the busy plaza.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the arch frames the cross so neatly that it looks like a painting. Then take a second one with the basilica towers behind.
card.good_to_know: The coral-stone pavilion was built in 1834 under Spanish rule. It holds the original wooden cross planted by Magellan's expedition when it reached Cebu on 21 April 1521. A tindalo-wood case was put around it in 1835 to stop people chipping off pieces. Together with the basilica, the pavilion became a National Cultural Treasure in 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Plaza Sugbo, next to the Basilica del Santo Niño. Walk about a minute south-east to just outside one of the pavilion's arches and face the cross.

card.hook: Cebu's biggest mall has a secret: the best photo isn't of the mall, it's from its roof. Up in the garden, the whole city spreads out around you.
card.stand_here: Head up to Sky Park, the rooftop garden on top of SM Seaside City, and stand right at the subject. Face the Busay side for the Cebu City skyline with the hills behind it. Turn the other way for the Mactan Channel and the CCLEX Bridge. The centre of the mall is a little to the east of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the skyline and the bridge. Go to 0.5x for the sweep of the garden. Then try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the CCLEX Bridge or the hills.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then tap the sky and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, before sunset, when the light is especially good and the open sky gives you lots of room to frame. Pick a clear day, because the view depends on the weather.
card.selfie_here: Go down to ground level and stand at the base of the Cube, the stainless-steel sculpture in front of the mall, which sources call the mall's signature photo spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn so the Cube is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the pedestrian overpass bridge that links the mall to its parking lot, where the Cube and the circular mall facade both fit in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Sky Park access, mall hours and the paid Skywalk Adventure can change, so check the official site before you go. The tall tower at the centre of the mall is closed to visitors, so don't count on it as a viewpoint.
card.challenge: Try a panorama from Sky Park: start with the city skyline, then slowly sweep round to the CCLEX Bridge without wobbling the phone.
card.good_to_know: SM Seaside City opened on 27 November 2015 and is the largest mall in Cebu, with a floor area of roughly 470,000 square metres. The Cube out front is a 21 x 21 metre stainless steel sculpture. For a calmer sea view, SRP Baywalk looks across the water to the bridge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to Sky Park, the rooftop garden on top of SM Seaside City, and stand right at the subject. Face the Busay side for the Cebu City skyline with the hills behind it. Turn the other way for the Mactan Channel and the CCLEX Bridge. The centre of the mall is a little to the east of you.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: you can fit the story of early Christian Cebu into a single photo, because the cross and the oldest church in the Philippines are only steps apart. No sprinting between sights required.
card.stand_here: Stand at Magellan's Cross, just outside the Basilica del Santo Niño near the main entrance. Face the basilica so the cross in its wooden housing is in front of you and the facade rises close behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the cross with the facade behind it. If the whole facade won't fit, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the belfry and facade details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the cross on one third of the frame and let the facade fill the rest, then tap the cross and make the shot a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the church.
card.best_time: Go early on a weekday for softer light and fewer people. If it's busy, wait a moment and the crowd usually shuffles out of your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza Hamabar, the small plaza near the basilica, where the belfry is in view behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and tap 0.5x if your phone has it so more of the tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the plaza in front of the church, so the whole facade and bell tower fit in the frame, while you stand with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't take photos while Mass is going on, and flash is often discouraged inside the church. Keep an eye on your belongings and watch out for pickpockets.
card.challenge: Get the cross on one third of the frame and the whole facade behind it, with no stranger's head sneaking into the shot.
card.good_to_know: This is the oldest church in the Philippines, founded in 1565 on the spot where the image of the Holy Child was rediscovered. The stone church you see today was completed in 1740. The 2013 Bohol earthquake badly damaged the belfry and facade, and the bell tower was fully restored by October 2016.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Magellan's Cross, just outside the Basilica del Santo Niño near the main entrance. Face the basilica so the cross in its wooden housing is in front of you and the facade rises close behind it.

card.hook: Picture a pale stone triangle sitting by the harbour, with green grass at its feet and one flagpole poking at the sky. Fort San Pedro is a gift for phone photos because the shapes are so clear.
card.stand_here: Walk round the outside of the walls to the grassy outer moat, then face the flagpole. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, and the Navigate buttons will take you there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big view of walls, flagpole and moat. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x, but keep the fort's edges away from the corners so the walls don't lean. Save zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the arched gate, the coat of arms and the stone texture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the base of the walls on the lower third, so the grass fills the bottom and the flagpole stands clear against the sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone than midday sun. Check the fort's opening hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stand under the arch at the main entrance gate, with the stone gate behind you and its coat of arms and flag above. Use your front camera, or 0.5x if your front camera has it, and let the gate loom over your shoulder. For a second option, try the flower-lined walkway with the old stone walls behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street side in front of the Cebu Central Post Office, right next to the fort, and shoot back toward the fort's outside walls while you pose in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay back from walls, edges and barriers, and don't lean on or climb anything. Some exhibits may restrict flash, so follow the signs and staff. The ramparts and interior need an admission ticket, and some parts have been damaged by storms and earthquakes, so check the official site before you visit.
card.challenge: Find the carved date on the gate and get it in the same frame as the coat of arms, with no tourists' elbows in the way (good luck).
card.good_to_know: The fort you see today dates from 1738, and the date is carved on the gate. It's described as the oldest triangular bastion fort in the country, and began as a wooden fort after Legazpi arrived in the 1560s. The walls are 6.1 metres high and 2.4 metres thick, and it became a National Cultural Treasure in 2020.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk round the outside of the walls to the grassy outer moat, then face the flagpole. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, and the Navigate buttons will take you there.

card.hook: Colon Street is loud, crowded and a bit run-down, and that's exactly why it photographs so well. Signs, shopfronts, vendors and passers-by all squeeze into one lively scene.
card.stand_here: Face down Colon, so the obelisk is in front of you and the street stretches away behind it, just like the old postcard.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the postcard view. Go to zoom 0.5x for the arch or a packed stretch of street, and zoom 2x or more to pick out the obelisk and its markers.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the obelisk on one of the vertical lines and keep the phone level so the shopfronts don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning light is a good match for the arch at the start of the street. If you're here between September and January, look out for the night market, which turns the street into a very different picture after dark.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the obelisk in the eastern part of the street, where a historical marker sits at its base. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the obelisk over your shoulder. The arch at the street entrance is a good photo spot too, ideally in the morning.
card.rules_and_safety: Crowds are part of the scene, and the area has a reputation for pickpockets. Keep your phone secure in your hand or a zipped pocket, and don't flash it around.
card.challenge: Find an old postcard or archive photo of the street online, hold it up next to the real view and snap your own then-and-now.
card.good_to_know: The street is named after Cristóbal Colón (Christopher Columbus) and was once the heart of Cebu City's shopping, offices and cinemas. You'll often hear it called the oldest street in the Philippines, but historians dispute that. The earliest map showing it dates from 1873, and the label seems to have started on postcards sold from 1910. A night market has run here several times a year since 2007.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map and stand across from the grey obelisk on Colon Street. Face down Colon, so the obelisk is in front of you and the street stretches away behind it, just like the old postcard.

card.hook: Red lanterns, a big Santo Niño statue and a wall of coral stone: the front of the Yap–San Diego House looks like a film set, and it's the real thing. It's thought to be among the oldest surviving Chinese houses outside China.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Mabini Street and Lopez Jaena Street, in the old Parián district, and face the front of the house where the stone walls and entrance meet the street. Heading north through Parián brings you to the front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front of the house. Only drop to 0.5x if the street is too narrow to fit it all in, and keep the house in the middle so it doesn't stretch. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the windows, roof edge and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap the brightest wall and slide it a little darker so the stone and wood keep their colour.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the front. Check locally for opening details before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head into the garden and sit on the bench next to the well in the corner, which is a spot visitors like for photos. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and tilt it so the house peeks over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the Lopez Jaena and Mabini Street corner and ask them to step back until the façade and its lanterns fill the frame, with you standing in front.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed, including inside, but ask before you take photos indoors. Skip the flash near delicate artefacts and religious statues.
card.challenge: Collect three textures in three taps: rough coral stone, old wood and the sloping roof edge. Bonus points if you can tell which is which without looking.
card.good_to_know: The house was probably built between 1675 and 1700 by Don Juan Yap, a merchant from Fujian, and his wife Doña Maria Florido. Parián was the quarter where Chinese residents had to live in Spanish colonial times. It's protected by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines, has been open to visitors since 2008, and a descendant of the original family still looks after it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Mabini Street and Lopez Jaena Street, in the old Parián district, and face the front of the house where the stone walls and entrance meet the street. Heading north through Parián brings you to the front.

card.hook: Most monuments give you one good angle. This one gives you a dozen, because it's a whole story of Cebu in bronze, brass, steel and concrete, packed with figures, a Spanish galleon and Magellan's Cross. Plan on a few pictures, not just one.
card.stand_here: Stand on P. Burgos Street, with the monument about 220 m to the north, and face north toward it. Hold your phone level and keep the whole structure in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full view from the street. Move to 0.5x when you're close and want the whole tableau in one shot. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for faces, figures and the galleon.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sculpture, then slide it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't turn the bronze into a dark silhouette.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening, when the light is softer and the monument may be lit up. If the lights are on, try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the church side of the monument in Parian Park and stand in front of the church-facade panel, with the relief church and the stone-column cross behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little low so the scene fills the frame behind your shoulder. Check on site, since there's no exact spot to point you to.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street from the monument, at Parian Plaza, and take a wide shot that fits in you, the whole sculpture, Parian Park and the street around it.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy part of the city, so keep your phone and bag secure. The monument has a fence around it, so check the official site before you go in case access has changed.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole monument, then find three different scenes up close and see if you can tell which one is the baptism of Rajah Humabon.
card.good_to_know: The monument tells Cebu's story from the Battle of Mactan in 1521 to the beatification of Pedro Calungsod in 2000. Sculptor Eduardo Castrillo designed it, and it was inaugurated on 8 December 2000. It stands on the former Plaza Parian, where the old San Juan Bautista Church once was, and is the centrepiece of Parian Park.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on P. Burgos Street, with the monument about 220 m to the north, and face north toward it. Hold your phone level and keep the whole structure in the frame.

selfie_spots.why: This face of the tableau has the most readable single backdrop, so a selfie taken here keeps a clear monument behind you, though no page names an exact standing point.

card.hook: Everybody lines up in the open square for the big front-on photo of Cebu's cathedral. Slip round to the side garden instead: you get leafy plants, old stone and far fewer people in your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon in the side garden beside Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral. Face the church wall and keep the plants low in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the garden and the wall together. If your phone has zoom 2x, use it to pick out the stonework without stepping into the planting. Save zoom 0.5x for the front square, where it squeezes in the whole façade and bell tower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the white walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go at golden hour, when the light turns soft and warm. It's lovely on the garden and the stonework.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, stand in the side corridor beside the white caryatid lamp posts, with the arched windows behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little low so the lamp posts and windows fit in. Or try the red plaza out front with the façade behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the plaza in front of the main façade, facing you, while you stand with the church behind you so the whole front fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church, so keep it quiet, skip the flash (especially during Mass) and ask before photographing other people. The area around is quite local and modest, so it's best not to show off anything flashy. Restoration work can change access, so check opening times before you go.
card.challenge: Hunt for the pair of griffins on the façade, then get them and your grin into the same shot.
card.good_to_know: A church for Saint Vitalis of Milan was first founded here in 1565, close to the Spanish fort, which makes this one of the oldest church sites in the Philippines. Wartime bombing left only the bell tower (dated 1835), the façade and the walls standing, and the rest was rebuilt in the 1950s. Those thick walls are the kind built to ride out typhoons.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon in the side garden beside Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral. Face the church wall and keep the plants low in your frame.

card.hook: Picture a 170-year-old house where the windows are made of shell and the afternoon light comes through them like a warm lamp. That's Casa Gorordo, and the wood, stone and glow do most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Head inside the museum compound in the old Parian district, go upstairs, and stand on the second-floor balcony (the veranda), right where the phone icon sits on the map. Look out or along the veranda so the wooden upper floor and the house details fill your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the balcony and the house details. Drop to zoom 0.5x in narrow rooms or to fit the whole veranda in. If your phone has zoom 2x, use it for carved wood and small details so you don't have to lean in.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of a shell window, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the windows keep their detail and the rooms stay warm.
card.best_time: Go early or late in the day, when the light on the wooden balcony is softer and tour groups are usually smaller. Hours can differ from place to place online, so check the museum's official site before you head over.
card.selfie_here: Try the green lawn of the garden courtyard with the house facade behind you, or the azotea, the open upper terrace overlooking the garden. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the old house over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a friendly passer-by, stand on the front lawn with the coral-stone facade behind you, and ask them to shoot from the street side so the whole front fits in (there's no official marked spot, so this is our best guess).
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine without flash, but some rooms have no-photography signs, so read each one. One visitor said videos weren't allowed, so ask staff. Commercial shoots need permission in advance, and pre-wedding shoots are not allowed on the premises.
card.challenge: Find a shell window and catch its glow falling on an old piece of furniture, with no flash and no people in the shot. Bonus points if the wood looks warm enough to touch.
card.good_to_know: Casa Gorordo was built in the 1850s by Alejandro Reynes y Rosales and later lived in by four generations of the Gorordo family, including Juan Gorordo, the first native Filipino bishop of Cebu. It's a classic balay nga tisa, a 'house with a tiled roof', that mixes native Filipino, Spanish colonial and Chinese looks. It came through World War II without structural damage and opened in December 1983 as Cebu's first public museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head inside the museum compound in the old Parian district, go upstairs, and stand on the second-floor balcony (the veranda), right where the phone icon sits on the map. Look out or along the veranda so the wooden upper floor and the house details fill your frame.
